headline: Hackers May Have Stolen Secret Keys from an AI Coding Tool Called OpenCode

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: OpenCode is a computer program that helps people write code using artificial intelligence, or AI, which is computer technology that can do tasks like a human brain, such as answering questions. Some people used a part of OpenCode called Console to save special passwords, called keys, that let them use AI tools made by other companies, like OpenAI and Google. On October 16, someone broke into an old part of OpenCode's computer system without permission. This could mean the keys some people saved were stolen. A key works like a secret code. If someone else gets it, they can use it to run up a bill on your account, just like someone using your allowance without asking. OpenCode told the people who might be affected to change their keys right away. Some users said money was already spent on their accounts without them knowing. This story matters because it shows why it is important to keep passwords and secret codes safe, and to change them quickly if something seems wrong.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: OpenCode is a tool that helps people write computer code with help from artificial intelligence (AI), which is technology built to think and respond somewhat like a human. Some OpenCode users paid for an extra feature called Console, where they stored secret access codes, called API keys, for AI companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. These keys let Console use those companies' AI tools on the users' behalf without showing the key to anyone else. On the night of October 16, someone broke into an old part of OpenCode's system without permission. This could have let the intruder see the stored keys. About 1.4% of Console users were affected, and OpenCode emailed them the next morning telling them to cancel their old keys and create new ones immediately. A stolen key is dangerous because whoever has it can use the AI service and the real owner gets charged for it, just like someone using your credit card without asking. Some users already reported unexpected charges, ranging from a few hundred dollars to over a thousand. OpenCode said the break-in seemed connected to something called a 'distillation attack,' where criminals use stolen access to copy an AI's answers on a massive scale in order to build a rival AI product. The company says it is still working with the AI companies to fix the problem and that attackers kept trying to break in again afterward. This story matters because it shows how even trusted apps can be hacked, and why people should always set spending limits and watch their accounts closely for strange charges.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: OpenCode makes software that helps programmers write code with assistance from artificial intelligence (AI), a type of technology that can analyze information and generate responses similarly to a human. One optional feature, called Console, lets teams store their own private access codes — called API keys — for outside AI companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. Console then uses those keys to run requests to the AI company on the user's behalf, so team members never have to see or handle the actual key themselves. On the night of October 16, someone broke into an older, less protected part of OpenCode's computer system. This intrusion may have exposed the keys that users had stored in Console. About 1.4% of Console users — everyone who had linked an outside AI key — were affected. The next morning, OpenCode emailed those users urging them to immediately cancel, or 'revoke,' their old keys with the AI companies and generate new ones, since simply deleting a key from Console does not actually cancel it with the provider. This matters because an API key works like a bearer credit card: whoever holds a copy can keep using it to run up charges until the original company cancels it. Several users reported real financial damage, with unauthorized usage charges ranging from a couple hundred dollars to as much as $1,700. OpenCode said the incident appeared linked to something called a 'distillation attack,' a scheme where attackers harvest huge numbers of an AI model's answers, often using stolen keys, login details, or fake accounts, in order to secretly train a competing AI model. The company has not explained exactly how its system was broken into, how long the intruder had access, or how many total users were impacted, though it says it is working with the AI companies involved to investigate and fix the issue. OpenCode's co-founder said attackers kept attempting new break-ins for days afterward, forcing the company to strengthen its security. This story is a useful reminder that digital 'keys' and passwords can be valuable targets for criminals, that companies should limit where sensitive credentials are stored, and that anyone using online services should monitor their accounts regularly and set spending alerts to catch unauthorized activity quickly.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: OpenCode provides software tools that help developers write code with the assistance of artificial intelligence (AI) models. One optional paid feature, called Console, allows teams to securely store API keys — unique digital credentials that grant access to AI services from companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google — so that team members can use those AI models without ever directly handling the sensitive key themselves. On the night of October 16, an unauthorized party accessed what the company described as a 'legacy system,' meaning an older piece of infrastructure, within OpenCode's network. This breach may have exposed the provider keys that users had uploaded to Console. Notably, OpenCode's standalone command-line and desktop applications were not affected, since those store keys locally on a user's own device rather than on OpenCode's servers. Roughly 1.4% of Console users — all of whom had linked an external AI key — were notified by email the following morning and instructed to revoke their existing keys immediately and generate replacements. This urgency stems from the nature of API keys as 'bearer credentials': anyone possessing a copy can submit billable requests to the AI provider under the original owner's account until that specific key is formally canceled. Simply deleting the key from OpenCode's Console interface does not revoke it at the provider level, and Console's own spending limits are powerless to stop unauthorized use, since Console can only monitor traffic passing through its own system. Several affected users have already reported real financial losses, including charges of a few hundred dollars up to $1,700, allegedly from unauthorized use of their OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google accounts. However, OpenCode has been careful to describe the keys only as having 'may have been exposed,' stopping short of confirming that any key was actually copied or misused. The company linked the breach to what it called a 'large-scale distillation attack' — a term referring to campaigns where bad actors extract enormous volumes of responses from an AI model, often using stolen credentials, fake accounts, or compromised payment methods, in order to train a competing model cheaply. OpenCode has not disclosed how the intruder initially gained access, how long the system was vulnerable, or precisely how many accounts were impacted. Its co-founder noted that attackers continued attempting new intrusions for at least two days after the breach was discovered, prompting the company to tighten security across its systems. This incident highlights a broader risk in the growing AI industry: as more services rely on shared credentials and cloud-based key storage, a single breach can have real financial consequences for ordinary users, and it underscores the importance of using unique keys per application, setting spending alerts, and reviewing account activity regularly.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: OpenCode offers developer tools that integrate artificial intelligence into the coding process. One of its offerings, Console, is an optional hosted service that lets teams centrally store API keys — the unique digital credentials required to authenticate requests to third-party AI providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google — so that individual team members can use those AI models without directly accessing the underlying key. On the night of October 16, an intruder gained access to what OpenCode described only as a 'legacy system,' an older component of its infrastructure, potentially exposing the provider keys stored within Console. The company has been explicit that this incident is distinct from its separate command-line and desktop applications, which store keys locally on users' own machines in a SQLite database and were therefore unaffected; as co-founder Dax Raad clarified, those locally stored keys 'never come to us.' Approximately 1.4% of Console users — specifically, those who had linked an external provider key — were notified by email on the morning of October 17 and instructed to revoke their compromised keys and issue replacements. The underlying danger is structural: an API key functions as a 'bearer credential,' meaning whoever physically possesses a copy of it can authorize billable requests against the original account holder's provider account until that specific key is invalidated by the provider itself. Deleting a key from within Console's interface has no effect on its validity with the provider, and Console's internal spending caps offer no protection either, since those caps only track traffic that passes through Console's own gateway rather than any unauthorized use occurring outside it. Several users have reported concrete financial harm as a result, with claimed unauthorized charges ranging from roughly $200 to as much as $1,700 across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google accounts. It is worth noting, however, that OpenCode's own public statements have consistently used hedged language — that keys 'may have been exposed' — without confirming that any specific key was actually copied, used, or misused. OpenCode connected the breach to what it termed a 'large-scale distillation attack,' a tactic in which actors systematically extract massive volumes of output from an AI model, frequently using networks of fraudulent accounts built with stolen payment information, compromised login credentials, or harvested API keys, in order to train a competing model at a fraction of its true development cost. Stolen keys also circulate on criminal marketplaces independent of any distillation effort, where they are resold or exploited simply to generate unauthorized usage charges. OpenCode has not disclosed how the legacy system was initially compromised, how long attackers had access before detection, the total number of affected accounts behind the 1.4% figure, or how the distillation campaign and the breach are definitively connected. Raad further noted that attackers continued persistent intrusion attempts against OpenCode's systems for at least 48 hours following initial detection, which prompted broader security hardening across the company's infrastructure. The episode illustrates a structural vulnerability increasingly common across the AI industry: as organizations centralize valuable, highly liquid credentials like API keys within third-party platforms, a single infrastructure failure can translate directly into real financial losses for end users, reinforcing the practical value of per-application key issuance, provider-side spending alerts, and routine billing audits as baseline security hygiene.

questions: If you used an online tool that stored a password or secret code for you, how would this story change how much you trust that company?
Why do you think it's important for companies to tell their users quickly when something like this happens, even if they don't have all the answers yet?
What steps could you take in your own life to protect accounts or passwords you use for school, games, or other online services?
